title: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
intro: This domain covers configuring Claude Code so it behaves consistently for a whole team and fits real delivery workflows: the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and modular organization, custom slash commands and skills with frontmatter controls, path-scoped rules, the plan mode versus direct execution decision, iterative refinement techniques, and headless integration into CI/CD pipelines. Exam questions frame these inside the Code Generation with Claude Code and Claude Code for CI scenarios, and reward knowing which mechanism — memory file, rule, skill, mode, or CLI flag — matches each requirement.

objectives.objective: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization
objectives.explanation:
Claude Code loads memory from a hierarchy of CLAUDE.md files: user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project-level (.claude/CLAUDE.md or a root CLAUDE.md), and directory-level files placed in subdirectories. The scoping rule that drives most exam scenarios is that user-level settings apply only to that user — instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are never shared with teammates via version control. When one developer's sessions follow the team's conventions and a new hire's do not, the diagnosis is almost always instructions living at user level instead of project level. The /memory command shows exactly which memory files are loaded, making it the first diagnostic step for inconsistent behavior across sessions or machines.

As projects grow, a monolithic CLAUDE.md becomes a liability: every session pays the token cost of standards that do not apply to the current work, and unrelated conventions bleed into tasks. Two mechanisms keep configuration modular. The @import syntax lets a CLAUDE.md reference external files, so each package's CLAUDE.md in a monorepo can import only the standards files relevant to that package — curated by the maintainers who actually know which standards apply. The .claude/rules/ directory organizes topic-specific rule files (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md) as an alternative to one giant file, and rule files can additionally be path-scoped (covered in objective 3.3).

The architect's decision is therefore twofold: put each instruction at the level where the right audience receives it (personal preferences at user level, team standards at project level, area-specific notes at directory level), and keep the content modular enough that sessions load relevant context rather than everything.
objectives.whyItMatters: Configuration hierarchy mistakes are silent: nothing errors, Claude just behaves differently on every laptop. Teams that keep shared conventions in version-controlled project-level files get consistent generation, deterministic onboarding, and reviewable changes to their standards; teams that let conventions live in individual home directories accumulate drift and re-teach the agent per developer, per session.

examples.title: Diagnosing the new hire whose sessions ignore team conventions
examples.body: A senior engineer's Claude Code sessions follow the team's error-handling standards, but a new hire cloning the same repo gets none of them. Running /memory on the senior engineer's machine shows the standards loading from ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — user-level configuration that never travels with the repository. The fix is moving the conventions into the project-level CLAUDE.md and committing it, so every clone receives them automatically. The /memory command then confirms both developers load identical memory files, and the class of per-machine drift disappears.

examples.title: Breaking up a 2,400-line monorepo CLAUDE.md with @import
examples.body: A six-package monorepo's root CLAUDE.md covers API standards, frontend conventions, migration rules, and deployment procedures for everything, so every session burns tokens on mostly irrelevant content. The team splits the standards into focused files and gives each package a CLAUDE.md that uses @import to pull in only the files relevant to that package — the API package imports api-conventions and error-handling, the frontend package imports component and styling standards. Package maintainers, who know their domain, own the import lists. Sessions load a fraction of the former context and stop mixing conventions across packages.

pitfalls: Putting team-wide conventions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — user-level files are not shared via version control, so teammates and new hires silently miss them.
Letting a single CLAUDE.md grow monolithic instead of using @import or .claude/rules/ — every session pays the token cost of irrelevant standards and conventions bleed between areas.
Skipping /memory when behavior differs between sessions or machines — it shows exactly which memory files loaded, and guessing instead wastes the diagnostic step the tool provides.
Duplicating the same conventions into multiple files or directories by hand rather than importing one shared source, which guarantees the copies drift apart.

objectives.objective: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills
objectives.explanation:
Custom slash commands live in two scopes: .claude/commands/ in the project is shared with the whole team via version control, while ~/.claude/commands/ holds personal commands that never leave the developer's machine. A command every developer should have after cloning the repo belongs in project scope; a private shortcut belongs in user scope. Skills live in .claude/skills/ as directories containing a SKILL.md file, and the SKILL.md frontmatter is the control surface for how a skill executes.

Three frontmatter options matter for the exam. context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, so skills that produce verbose output (codebase analysis) or exploratory context (brainstorming alternatives) do not pollute the main conversation — only the result comes back. allowed-tools restricts which tools the skill may use during execution, for example limiting a report-writing skill to file-write operations so it cannot take destructive actions. argument-hint prompts developers for required parameters when they invoke the skill without arguments. Developers who want to tweak a shared skill without affecting teammates create a personal variant in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name.

The final judgment call is skills versus CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md content is always loaded — the right home for universal standards that must shape every session. Skills are invoked on demand — the right home for task-specific workflows used occasionally. Putting an occasional workflow in CLAUDE.md wastes tokens in every session; putting universal conventions in a skill means they only apply when someone remembers to invoke it.
objectives.whyItMatters: Commands and skills are how proven workflows become shared, versioned team assets instead of personal prompt folklore. Getting scope wrong means teammates silently lack tooling; getting frontmatter wrong means verbose skills exhaust the main context or, worse, run with tool access they should never have.

examples.title: Hardening a codebase-analysis skill with frontmatter
examples.body: A team's analysis skill floods the main conversation with thousands of lines of discovery output, and in one run it edited source files when it should only write a report into docs/. The fix is two frontmatter lines in SKILL.md: context: fork, so the exploration runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only the summary returns to the main session, and allowed-tools restricted to the file-write operations the report requires, so destructive modifications become impossible rather than merely discouraged. An argument-hint entry additionally prompts for the target module when developers invoke the skill bare.

examples.title: Splitting always-on standards from a once-a-sprint workflow
examples.body: A retail team has naming and error-handling conventions that must shape every generated file, plus a multi-step release-notes workflow run once per sprint. The conventions go into the project CLAUDE.md, where they load into every session automatically. The release-notes procedure becomes a project-scoped skill: versioned, shared through the repo, and loaded only when invoked, so ordinary sessions never carry its token weight. Each asset now uses the loading model that matches how often it applies.

pitfalls: Creating team commands in ~/.claude/commands/ — user scope is personal, so the command never reaches teammates; shared commands belong in .claude/commands/ in the repo.
Running verbose or exploratory skills without context: fork, letting their output pollute and exhaust the main conversation's context window.
Omitting allowed-tools on skills that only need narrow access, leaving them free to take destructive actions the workflow never required.
Encoding universal coding standards as a skill — on-demand invocation means the standards silently do not apply in every session where nobody invokes the skill.

objectives.objective: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading
objectives.explanation:
Files in .claude/rules/ can carry YAML frontmatter with a paths field containing glob patterns, such as paths: ["terraform/**/*"]. A path-scoped rule loads only when Claude is editing files that match its globs. This gives two benefits: sessions that never touch matching files carry none of the rule's content, reducing irrelevant context and token usage, and the loading is deterministic — driven by file paths, not by the model inferring which section of a big CLAUDE.md applies.

The key architectural comparison is against directory-level CLAUDE.md files. Directory files scope instructions to one location in the tree, which works when an area of the codebase is physically contained in one directory. But many conventions follow file type rather than location: test files like Button.test.tsx co-located next to their components throughout the codebase, or generated files scattered across packages. A glob pattern such as **/*.test.tsx matches those files wherever they live, with one rule file to maintain. Achieving the same coverage with directory-level CLAUDE.md files would mean duplicating the conventions into every directory containing a test and keeping all the copies in sync.

When a path-scoped rule fails to activate, check the glob against where matching files actually live — a rule scoped to src/tests/** does nothing for co-located tests spread through src/. And resist the temptation to fix a non-loading rule by deleting the frontmatter: unconditional loading works, but it surrenders the token savings and scoping that motivated the rule in the first place.
objectives.whyItMatters: Path-scoped rules are how large codebases keep conventions accurate without bloating every session. Teams that scope by glob get the right conventions exactly when relevant files are edited; teams that pile everything into root CLAUDE.md pay tokens for irrelevant rules in every session and rely on the model to guess which section applies.

examples.title: Scoping Terraform conventions out of frontend sessions
examples.body: An insurance company's Terraform conventions — module structure, state management, tagging — live in the root CLAUDE.md and load into every session, including frontend work where they occasionally bleed into suggestions. The team moves them to .claude/rules/terraform.md with frontmatter paths: ["terraform/**/*"]. Now the conventions load only when Claude edits files under terraform/, frontend sessions shed the token overhead entirely, and the rule file remains versioned and shared through the repository like any other project configuration.

examples.title: Fixing a testing rule that never loads for co-located tests
examples.body: A media company scoped .claude/rules/testing.md to paths: ["src/tests/**"], but its tests are co-located — Player.test.tsx sits beside Player.tsx across dozens of directories — so the rule almost never activates and generated tests ignore the mocking standards. Changing the glob to ["**/*.test.tsx"] matches test files by type regardless of directory. This is precisely where glob-pattern rules beat directory-level CLAUDE.md files: one rule covers files spread across the whole tree, with no duplicated convention text to keep in sync.

pitfalls: Using directory-level CLAUDE.md files for conventions that follow file type across many directories — you end up duplicating and synchronizing the same text everywhere a matching file lives.
Writing globs that assume a layout the codebase does not have (e.g., scoping tests to src/tests/** when tests are co-located), so the rule silently never loads.
Removing paths frontmatter to force a rule to load — it works, but converts a scoped rule back into always-on context and forfeits the token savings.
Leaving convention text in root CLAUDE.md after migrating it to rules, so sessions double-load the content and the two copies drift.

objectives.objective: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution
objectives.explanation:
Plan mode is designed for complex work: large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications. It lets Claude explore the codebase safely and produce a design before any change is committed, which prevents costly rework when a mid-implementation discovery would otherwise invalidate work already done. Direct execution is appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes — a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace, adding one validation conditional — where planning overhead buys nothing.

The signals for plan mode read directly from the task: microservice restructuring, a library migration touching 45+ files, or a feature with competing integration approaches that have different infrastructure requirements. The signals for direct execution are equally concrete: the scope is one file or one function, the change is well understood, and there is essentially one reasonable way to do it. The two modes also combine: plan mode for investigation and approach selection, then direct execution to implement the committed plan.

The supporting mechanism to know is the Explore subagent. Discovery on a large codebase generates verbose output — file listings, grep results, long reads — that can exhaust the main conversation's context before implementation starts. The Explore subagent isolates that discovery in its own context and returns summaries, preserving the main window for the phases that follow. Reaching for it during multi-phase tasks is the difference between thorough exploration and a session that forgets its own findings.
objectives.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong mode costs real money in both directions: direct execution on architectural work produces half-migrated codebases that need rework when the approach proves wrong, while plan mode on trivial fixes adds ceremony that trains developers to skip planning even when it matters. Context exhaustion during discovery quietly degrades everything downstream.

examples.title: Planning a 45-file HTTP client migration before touching code
examples.body: A logistics team must replace a deprecated HTTP client across 45+ files, with two viable integration approaches that differ in retry and connection-pooling behavior. Starting direct execution file by file risks discovering mid-migration that the chosen pattern conflicts with production pooling — rework across every file already edited. Instead the engineer enters plan mode: Claude explores the call sites, compares the approaches against the infrastructure constraints, and produces a migration plan. Only then does implementation proceed in direct execution, following the committed design.

examples.title: Using the Explore subagent to survive a multi-phase modernization
examples.body: During discovery on a sprawling legacy codebase, file listings and long reads nearly exhaust the session's context before implementation begins, and the model starts losing earlier findings. Delegating discovery to the Explore subagent moves the verbose exploration into an isolated context; only summarized findings return to the main conversation. The main session retains room for planning and implementation, and the summaries preserve exactly the knowledge the later phases need.

pitfalls: Starting direct execution on tasks with unmade architectural decisions, letting implementation 'reveal' the approach — discoveries then invalidate work already completed.
Using plan mode reflexively for single-file, well-understood fixes, adding overhead that erodes the team's willingness to plan when it actually matters.
Running verbose discovery in the main conversation during multi-phase tasks instead of delegating to the Explore subagent, exhausting context before implementation.
Treating plan mode and direct execution as exclusive rather than sequencing them: plan the investigation-heavy phase, then execute the committed plan directly.

objectives.objective: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement
objectives.explanation:
Iterative refinement is a toolkit, and the exam tests matching the technique to the failure mode. When prose descriptions of a transformation are interpreted inconsistently — each attempt splitting a field differently, formatting dates another way — the most effective fix is 2-3 concrete input/output examples. A real input and its expected output settle ambiguities that no amount of stricter prose resolves, which is also why specific test cases with example input and expected output are the fastest way to fix edge-case handling like null values in migration scripts.

Test-driven iteration extends this: write the test suite first, covering expected behavior, edge cases, and performance requirements, then iterate by sharing test failures with Claude so each round is guided by concrete, verifiable gaps. It presumes you can specify expected behavior up front. When you cannot — the domain is unfamiliar and you do not yet know what questions to ask — use the interview pattern instead: have Claude ask you questions before implementing, surfacing considerations you had not anticipated, such as cache invalidation strategies or failure modes.

Finally, sequence fixes deliberately. When multiple issues interact — fixing one changes the right fix for another — present them together in a single detailed message so Claude can resolve them coherently. When issues are independent, fix them sequentially; batching unrelated problems dilutes attention on each.
objectives.whyItMatters: Refinement technique choice determines how many iterations a task takes and whether it converges at all. Teams that pin down ambiguity with examples, drive iteration with failing tests, and surface unknowns through interviews converge in a few rounds; teams that respond to every miss with longer prose re-prompts loop indefinitely on the same misinterpretations.

examples.title: Replacing three paragraphs of prose with two worked records
examples.body: A data engineer's prose specification for a legacy-record conversion keeps producing divergent scripts — one run splits addresses on commas, the next on line breaks. Instead of rewriting the prose more sternly, she provides two real legacy records alongside exactly the converted output each should produce, including one record with a null middle name and a multi-line address. The examples settle the delimiter question and the null handling at once, and the next generation of the script matches the expected outputs on the first try.

examples.title: Interviewing before building an unfamiliar caching layer
examples.body: A developer who has never built a caching layer plans to prompt 'add Redis caching to the records service' and iterate. Because he cannot yet articulate invalidation, staleness, or failure requirements, refinement would just orbit an unspecified design. He instead asks Claude to interview him first: the questions surface what happens when the cache is down, which endpoints tolerate stale reads, and how writes invalidate entries. The answers become the specification, and implementation starts from surfaced requirements rather than discovering them through failed iterations.

pitfalls: Responding to inconsistent outputs with longer, sterner prose instead of providing 2-3 concrete input/output examples that actually disambiguate the requirement.
Applying test-driven iteration in domains where you cannot yet specify expected behavior — write tests once the interview pattern has surfaced the requirements.
Fixing interacting issues one at a time, so each fix invalidates the last; interacting problems belong together in a single detailed message.
Batching independent issues into one sprawling message, diluting attention on each — independent problems iterate better sequentially.

objectives.objective: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines
objectives.explanation:
Headless operation starts with the -p (or --print) flag: Claude Code processes the prompt, writes the result to stdout, and exits, instead of waiting for interactive input that will never come in a pipeline. Without it, CI jobs hang indefinitely. For output that scripts must consume, --output-format json combined with --json-schema enforces structured, machine-parseable findings at the CLI level — the reliable basis for automation like posting inline PR comments, versus scraping free-form prose or hoping a prompt-level 'respond in JSON' instruction holds.

Context is what separates useful CI reviews from noisy ones. CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude Code project context: testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria documented there improve test generation quality and reduce low-value output. Providing existing test files in context prevents test generation from suggesting duplicate scenarios the suite already covers. And when reviews re-run after new commits, include the prior review's findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues — otherwise every push re-posts the same comments and buries fresh feedback.

One more property to design around: session context isolation. The same Claude session that generated code retains its generation reasoning and is less effective at reviewing its own changes; an independent review instance without that context catches issues the generator rationalizes away. In CI, generation and review should be separate invocations.
objectives.whyItMatters: CI integrations run unattended at high volume: a hanging job blocks every merge, unparseable output breaks the automation consuming it, and duplicate or low-value findings train developers to ignore the bot entirely. The CLI flags and context practices here are the difference between a review step teams trust and one they disable within a month.

examples.title: Wiring an automated PR reviewer into GitHub Actions
examples.body: A DevOps engineer's first attempt at a review job hangs waiting for input and emits prose the posting script cannot parse. The fix is two CLI changes: run claude with -p so the prompt executes non-interactively and the process exits, and add --output-format json with --json-schema so findings arrive as structured objects with file, line, severity, and message fields. The posting script then maps each finding to an inline PR comment directly, with no regex scraping and no risk of a malformed prose response breaking the pipeline.

examples.title: Stopping a review bot from re-posting the same findings
examples.body: An e-commerce team's bot re-runs on every push and re-posts identical findings, burying new feedback — one comment appears four times. The pipeline is changed to fetch the findings already posted on the PR and include them in the new run's context, with instructions to report only new issues or previously raised issues that remain unaddressed. Duplicates stop at the source, and the bot's confirmation of which earlier findings are resolved becomes useful signal in itself.

pitfalls: Omitting -p in pipeline invocations, so the CI job hangs waiting for interactive input that never arrives.
Relying on prompt-level 'respond only in JSON' instructions instead of --output-format json with --json-schema — probabilistic formatting eventually breaks the consuming script.
Re-running reviews without prior findings in context, flooding pull requests with duplicate comments as commits accumulate.
Letting the same session that generated code review its own changes — session context isolation means an independent instance reviews more effectively.
Skipping CLAUDE.md documentation of testing standards and available fixtures, then wondering why CI-generated tests are low-value or duplicate existing coverage.
